stimulus.text: Paraphrase: By the end of 1943, American forces in the Pacific were using a strategy called 'island hopping.' Instead of attacking every Japanese-held island, they seized only the islands that mattered most, such as airfields and positions that could block enemy ships. Islands they skipped were cut off by blockade, so the Japanese forces left on them, in the words of the time, 'withered on the vine.' Marines landed on Guadalcanal in August 1942, the first American offensive in the Pacific, and months of jungle fighting followed before the Japanese withdrew in February 1943.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary summary drawn from Barron's Chapter 9 ('Island Hopping'; Guadalcanal) and 5 Steps Chapter 24.

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded figures and paraphrases (see source_note)
stem: Why did American planners prefer to blockade the islands they skipped rather than attack them?

options.text: The skipped islands had no Japanese soldiers stationed on them at all
options.misconception: Skipped islands held Japanese garrisons; blockade cut off their supplies.

options.text: Attacking fortified islands cost lives and time, while blockade starved the garrisons
American ships could not reach the skipped islands in the Pacific
options.misconception: American ships reached the islands to blockade them; they chose not to land.

options.text: The Japanese had already agreed to surrender those islands to the Allies
options.misconception: Japan never agreed to surrender those islands; they were starved out.

rationales.A: Skipped islands held Japanese garrisons, cut off from supplies.
rationales.B: Blockade starved the garrisons without the cost of an assault.
rationales.C: American ships reached the islands to blockade them.
rationales.D: Japan never agreed to surrender those islands.
rationales.general:
1. The passage says island hopping skipped the most heavily fortified islands.
2. Attacking a fortified island meant heavy losses for the attackers.
3. Background from the books: blockade cut off supply ships, so the bypassed garrisons 'withered on the vine.'
4. Skipping the island achieved the same result as taking it, at far lower cost.
Remember: a siege can beat an assault, so ask whether a target must be taken or only neutralized.
